## Paper

## Abstract

Superconductivity, characterized by dissipationless current flow with flux expulsion or quantization, is usually suppressed when the magnetic field or the temperature is sufficiently high. However, in rare instances, superconductivity can reappear upon increasing the temperature or magnetic field, a phenomenon known as reentrant superconductivity. It usually emerges from competing orders in strongly correlated materials. Here we demonstrate reentrant superconductivity as a function of both temperature and magnetic field, tuned by radio-frequency power in a relatively simple system: granular aluminum, which exhibits the properties of a naturally occurring Josephson junction array. At low temperatures, giant Shapiro steps emerge, exhibiting characteristics of a single Josephson junction. Coherent phase locking across the array’s multiple junctions amplif ies the quantized voltage, enabling tunability at radio frequencies, as observed in artificially designed Josephson arrays. We show that our system can be tuned from a coherent superconducting (stiff-phase) to an insulating (phase-fluctuating) state using radio-frequency power. We propose that radio-frequency power modulates the Josephson coupling energy, 𝐸 . Remarkably, at elevated temperatures, the screening of the electron charge suppresses the charging energy, causing superconductivity to reappear. This many-body effect cannot be described within a single junction framework and involves many-body correlations. Our system can therefore be tuned to observe both the single-junction regime and many-body correlation effects, serving as a quantum simulator for complex phenomena in condensed matter physics.

---

## Introduction

Complex behavior can arise in large networks governed by simple rules1, a principle observed across physics in phenomena such as spontaneous magnetization in Ising models, phase transitions in percolation theory, and synchronization in coupled oscillators2. One prominent example of a quantum network exhibiting such emergent behavior is the Josephson junction (JJ) array, which offers a rich platform for exploring collective quantum dynamics3. In this correlated quantum system, the relevant energy scales are the Josephson coupling across the junction 𝐸 = \hbar I_c / 2e, which determines the confinement of the Josephson phase, and the charging energy 𝐸 = e^2 / 2C, which determines the strength of Coulomb interactions, with I being the Junction’s critical current and C the capacitance. The interplay between these energy scales yields a superconductor-to-insulator quantum phase transition4, obtained for 𝐸 \simeq 𝐸 .

Reentrant superconductivity is a phenomenon in which the superconducting phase unexpectedly reappears from a dissipative state when increasing a tuning parameter of the system, such as temperature, magnetic field, and pressure. It has been observed in systems including superconductor-ferromagnet compounds5–8 and layered structures9,10, bismuthates 11, heavy-fermions12,13, Kagome materials14, topological insulator JJs15, and twisted moiré materials16. This phenomenon often arises from competing orders, such as ferromagnetism and superconductivity in ErRh4B4 and HoMo6S8 5,8, charge density waves and superconductivity in ZrTe 17, or different pairing mechanisms in UTe 13 and magic-angle graphene13,18. Reentrant superconductivity has also been ex plored through gauge-gravity duality, where black hole stability serves as a probe of holographic superconductivity in the dual non-relativistic field theory19.

Theoretically, it has been shown that within a specific regime of the quantum coupling ratio, 𝐸 /𝐸 , reentrant superconductivity can emerge in JJ arrays20. At moderate temperatures, quasiparticle screening reduces 𝐸 , enabling charge fluctuations and the reappearance of superconductivity. As the temperature decreases, this screening effect diminishes, restoring 𝐸 and driving the system back into a phase-fluctuating, dissipative state20,21. Despite its theoretical foundation, this reentrant behavior has remained experimentally elusive due to limitations in fabricating artificial JJ arrays with the required precision.

Various methods have been employed to tune 𝐸 /𝐸 in JJ arrays. For instance, varying the insulating barrier thickness to tune junction resistance22, tuning junction critical current with a magnetic field23, gating a two-dimensional electron gas placed in a proximity to the array to affect its screening24, and electron depletion in semiconductor-superconductor hybrid devices25. While these methods could effectively tune 𝐸 /𝐸 across the superconductor-to-insulator transition, only traces for quasi-reentrant behavior were observed experimentally22,26. A clear reappearance of a dissipationless superconducting state in a JJ array is still lacking.

We have employed a new approach for realizing a JJ array and for tuning its parameters. We utilize a naturally occurring JJ array made of granular aluminum (grAl). This material consists of superconducting islands coupled through insulating interlayers27 (See Figure 1c for illustration). The grain size and the barrier strength are controlled by the deposition conditions28,29. The system features nanoscale grain size, making the strong quantum fluctuations regimes of both charge and phase accessible30. Compared to artificial JJ arrays, the significantly smaller grain size results in a longer screening length, enhancing correlations between junctions across the array. Additionally, the electronic level spacing within each island exceeds both 𝐸 and the superconducting gap31–33. This strong separation makes the system less sensitive to microscopic details34, as disorder typically results in level broadening. Therefore, it is a promising building block for high kinetic inductance and low-loss quantum devices34. Finally, to control the Josephson parameters, we adapted a new approach by application of radio frequency (RF) power to tune the critical current 𝐼 35, thereby varying 𝐸 . The drive frequency should be much smaller compared to the characteristic frequency of the junction 𝜔 ~\sqrt{E_J E_C}, so it is mainly 𝐼 that depends on the RF amplitude36 (See Fig. 1c for illustration of the set-up and our interpretation for the effect of the RF power on junction properties and the quantum phase slip rate). Utilizing the unique properties of grAl and our new tuning approach, we can tune through the various regimes of the device. We realize a superconductor-to-insulator transition as a function of RF power with a strong insulating state. This insulator has ten times higher resistance compared with the device normal resistanceand the derivative of the device resistance with respect to temperature is negative (see Supplementary Information Fig. S5). In addition, in the insulator regime we observe a pronounced temperature dependent reentrant superconductivity. We explain our data using two regimes: at low temperatures, the system is described as a phase locked JJ array featuring giant Shapiro steps, obeying single-junction-type physics. At high temperatures, the reentrant behavior is described within the many-body correlated picture suggested by Efetov20, where reentrance is induced by the screening of long-range interactions. Our findings emphasize the potential of using granular superconductors as controlled platforms for developing novel quantum devices and exploring emergent quantum phenomena in strongly correlateNd systems.

---

## Results

RF tuned superconductor-to-insulator transition

We study a JJ array implemented using a superconducting nanobridge fabricated from a grAl thin film (Fig. 1c). The nanobridge has a length of ℓ ≃ 120 nm, width 𝑤 ≃ 200 nm, and thickness 𝑡 ≃ 55 nm. These dimensions are significantly larger than the grain size of grAl, 𝑑 = 2±0.5 nm,37 the inter-grain spacing (𝑠 ≃ 1 nm), and the superconducting coherence length (𝜉 ≃ 10 nm) 38. Additionally, the bridge dimensions are much smaller than the in-plane magnetic penetration depth (𝜆 ≃ 1 μm) 39, resulting in a relatively uniform current distribution along the array40. Naively, the bridge would consist of approximately 𝑁 ×𝑁 ×𝑁 ≃ 40×67×18 inter-grain JJs. However, the effective number of junctions can differ significantly due to additional contributions coming from the contact region41.

We begin by demonstrating the tunability of the system at a low temperature of 𝑇 = 50 mK as shown in Fig. 1a. The differential resistance 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 is shown to be tunable by the RF power 𝑃 and the bias current 𝐼 . Below a critical power 𝑃 (𝑃 < 𝑃 = −13 dBm), the superconducting state (blue region) is observed for low bias currents, where a typical suppression of the critical current is observed. Upon increasing the power at zero bias (𝐼 ≃ 0), a peak in the differential resistance emerges. This peak reaches its maximum height and minimum width at 𝑃 = −10.5 dBm, which we define as the insulating state (I). We note that the zero-bias resistance 𝑅 is an order of magnitude larger than the resistance in the normal state 𝑅 , obtained at the highest DC currents and RF powers where superconductivity is completely quenched. Furthermore, when raising the temperature, 𝑅 decreases, a typical behavior for an insulating state. Previous studies on JJ arrays 42,43 and single junctions44 have reported power-induced transitions to a resistive state characterized by Shapiro step behavior. In contrast, the power-driven transition to an insulating state observed here is significantly more pronounced.

Upon increasing 𝐼 and 𝑃 further, clear oscillations of 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 are observed. We interpret these oscillations as giant Shapiro steps, as evidenced from our further analysis in Fig. 3. These Shapiro steps demonstrate that the low temperature dependence of the system can be described within an effective single JJ model as described in the theoretical analysis below and depicted in Fig. 1d.

Reentrant superconductivity

We now look at the 𝑃−𝑇 phase diagram of the system, shown in Fig. 1b. We observe reentrant superconductivity as a function of temperature; this is our main result. This phenomenon has been predicted by Efetov for an array of JJ’s as depicted in Fig. 1e. In our case we conjecture that a finite RF power is needed for carefully tuning 𝐸 for one to be able to observe the reentrance behavior as will be discussed further below.

For illustration, let us first follow the dashed line in Fig. 1b at 𝑃 = −14.25 dBm: at low temperatures, the system is superconducting with 𝑅 = 0. As the temperature increases above 1.5 K, 𝑅 goes through a peak: this is the insulating state. Upon increasing the temperature further, superconductivity surprisingly reappears, this being the reentrant superconducting phase SRC 2. Above 2.5 K, the normal state N of the system is observed. As noted above, the normal state resistance of the array is an order of magnitude smaller than the insulating state resistance.

The various regimes of the system, SC 1, I, SC 2, and N, are indicated on the phase diagram. Remarkably, we observe reentrant superconductivity as a function of temperature. For 𝑃 < 𝑃, the system undergoes from low 𝑇 superconductivity (SC 1) to high 𝑇 superconductivity (SC 2), while crossing through the insulating (I) regime. In the insulating regime, 𝑅(𝑇) is first rising with lowering 𝑇, then saturating at low 𝑇. This saturation at the lowest temperatures may not be an intrinsic property of the system but a result of the electronic heat generated by the RF power 45 (see Supplementary Information Sec. Ⅴ.B).

To investigate the effect of RF power and bias current, we fix the RF power at 𝑃 = −14.25 dBm, and plot the differential resistance 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 as a function of bias current 𝐼 and temperature 𝑇 (see Fig. 2a-b). As the temperature increases, the critical current 𝐼 of the superconducting state SC 1 decreases rapidly and vanishes completely at 𝑇 = 1.35 K. Upon increasing the temperature further, the resistance rises, reaching a peak in the zero-bias resistance around 𝑇 = 1.8 K.

Along the 𝐼 axis, (i.e., with increasing bias current), we observe oscillations in 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 (Shapiro steps). At 𝑇 = 2.16 K, the critical current 𝐼 reappears, signaling the onset of a reentrant superconducting phase (SC 2), which forms a dome-shaped region in the 𝐼 −𝑇 diagram at fixed RF power.

Fig. 2b, highlights this reentrant regime, where SC 2 is clearly visible. For comparison, Fig. 2c shows measurements taken without RF power, displaying a conventional 𝐼 (𝑇) dependence without reentrance. As discussed further below, we propose that the presence of RF power is essential for fine-tuning the effective coupling energy 𝐸 .

Giant Shapiro steps

The dependence of the system response on the RF frequency, 𝑓 , is explored in Fig. 3. We study the differential resistance 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 as a function of 𝐼 and 𝑓 , focusing on the insulating state, Fig. 3a-b. 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 exhibits damped oscillations as a function of 1/𝑓 , Fig. 3a. The oscillations are smeared at low frequencies, while the insulator zero-bias peak is enhanced (see inset), suggesting it has a different origin.

Looking at the 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 in the 𝑓 −𝑉 plane, Fig. 3b, we reveal the origin of the oscillations. They follow the giant Shapiro steps relation42, 𝑉 = 𝑛𝑁𝜙 𝑓 . Here 𝑛 is an integer, 𝜙 is the flux quantum, and 𝑁 is the number of phase locked junctions connected in series. Using the frequency dependence, we obtain contributions from 𝑁 = 430 junctions, which exceeds the number of junctions in the nanobridge (𝑁 ). This difference can be attributed to an extended phase drop across the device41, which comprises the nanobridge in series with long grAl contacts (see Supplementary Information Sec. Ⅴ.C and Fig. S7).

At a given frequency, the first consecutive Shapiro steps are missing. As the frequency decreases, more steps are hidden by the insulator peak, and only higher harmonic steps are visible. This behavior contrasts with the regular giant Shapiro steps that cross the origin in the frequency-voltage plane, as typically observed in JJ arrays43. Fig. 3c shows the giant Shapiro steps observed at 𝑓 = 67.5 MHz. They clearly illustrate the even-odd effect expected for the current step width46. They are characterized by a finite voltage width expected for arrays with minuscule disorder47 (see Supplementary Information Sec. Ⅴ.C).

We extend our investigation by examining the RF response of the system under an external magnetic field (Fig. 4). At low temperatures and at zero fields, we define 𝑃 = −13 dBm and 𝑃 = −10.5 dBm at the onset of SC 1 and the insulating (I) regimes, respectively. They exhibit non-monotonic modulation by the out-of-plane magnetic field 𝜇 𝐻 (Fig. 4a). The oscillations of the critical power 𝑃 are reminiscent of a Fraunhofer-type interference. The oscillatory, non-monotonic behavior of 𝑃 as a function of magnetic field, along with the strong suppression of 𝑅 at small 𝜇 𝐻 , suggests that the insulating phase emerges from the superconducting state.

In contrast, when an in-plane magnetic field 𝜇 𝐻 , aligned with the current direction, is applied, both 𝑃 and 𝑃 decrease monotonically, while 𝑅 is suppressed only at significantly higher fields (Fig. 4b). In both magnetic field orientations, and within the power range 𝑃 < 𝑃 < 𝑃, distinct resistance oscillations are observed. These oscillations correspond to the missing Shapiro steps, which reemerge once the zero-bias peak associated with the insulating state is suppressed by the magnetic field.

Remarkably, at elevated temperatures, we observe signatures of field-induced reentrant superconductivity, most prominently under in-plane field conditions (Fig. 4c-d). This reentrance may be consistent with Efetov’s picture: here, quasiparticles would be produced by pair-breaking48,49, enhancing screening, when the applied magnetic field is close to the upper critical field38.

Theoretical model

For simplicity, we conceptualize our system as a stack of many parallel one-dimensional chains of JJs. This model captures the Shapiro steps observed in Fig. 1a at low temperature and RF frequencies well below 𝜔 , using effective single-junction physics, as we now explain. The semiclassical equation of motion for each junction is given by the model of a resistively and capacitively shunted junction (RCSJ) under simultaneous DC and RF bias,

𝛽 \frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial\tau^2} + \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\tau} + \sin\phi = i_0 + i_1 \sin(\Omega\tau), (1)

where 𝛽 = 2𝜋𝑅^2𝐶𝐼 /𝜙 is set by the normal resistance 𝑅, the capacitance 𝐶, and the critical current 𝐼 of the junction. The time 𝑡 has been rescaled by 𝑡 = 𝜙 /(2𝜋𝑅𝐼 ) to define the dimensionless parameter 𝜏 = 𝑡/𝑡 , 𝛺 = 𝜔 𝑡 is the rescaled RF frequency, and 𝑖 = 𝐼 /𝐼 , 𝑖 = 𝐼 /𝐼 are the rescaled DC and RF currents, respectively (the latter being proportional to the square root of the RF power, 𝐼 ∼ \sqrt{P}).

The voltage drop across the junction is given by 𝑉 = 𝜙 \partial_t \phi/2𝜋. We assume that the DC and RF currents flowing through the sample are distributed equally between the one-dimensional chains; then, within each chain, the RCSJ equations decouple, and the total voltage drop across the chain is given by the voltage drop across a single junction multiplied by the number of junctions in each chain.

In Fig. 1d, we present calculations of 𝑑𝑣/𝑑𝑖 as a function of the rescaled DC current 𝑖 and RF power 𝑃, where 𝑣 = \partial_\tau \phi = 2𝜋𝑡 𝑉/𝜙 is the rescaled voltage, obtained for 𝛺 = 0.1 and 𝛽 = 1 (see Supplementary Information Sec. Ⅲ for extended discussion and other parameter regimes). While the model is simplified, it captures the Shapiro steps observed in Fig. 1a; this is in line with previous studies of JJ arrays42. Moreover, it accounts for the oscillatory behavior seen as a function of temperature in Fig. 2a: temperature reduces the critical current such that 𝑖 = 𝐼 /𝐼 (𝑇) in Eq. (1) become temperature-dependent, leading to the emergence of Shapiro steps.

## Methods

Device fabrication

The naturally occurring JJ arrays have been implemented by granular aluminum nanobridge devices. The nanobridges were obtained using standard liftoff electron beam lithography. Device dimensions were examined by atomic force microscopy. Granular aluminum thin films were thermally evaporated on R-plane sapphire substrates held at liquid nitrogen temperature. Compared to films deposited on substrates held at room temperature, this approach reduces the mean grain size and narrows the grain size distribution29. For the nanobridge device presented in the main text, the film resistivity is 𝜌 = 2800 μΩcm, estimated by measuring an on-chip Hall bar device at room temperature. Measurements in additional devices are discussed in Supplementary Information Sec. Ⅴ.E. We employ a quasi-four-probe measurement configuration, where the granular aluminum nanobridge is connected in series with wide superconducting granular aluminum contacts (see Fig. S11a).

Measurement setup

Measurements were conducted in a dilution refrigerator with a base temperature of 20 mK and a (8 T,1 T,1 T) superconducting vector magnet. DC transport measurements were taken while simultaneously applying RF signals characterized by a power, 𝑃 (dBm), defined in the signal generator output. The measurement setup is illustrated in Supplementary Information Fig. S11b. The DC lines are filtered using a multi-stage RF and DC low-pass filter mounted on the mixing chamber plate, followed by additional DC low-pass filtering on the sample board, thereby reducing injected RF noise and ensuring that only the DC voltage is measured. The RF lines are attenuated at different stages of the dilution refrigerator and are coupled to the device through on-board RF bias-tees. The bias tees consist of a 50 kΩ DC bias resistor and a 22 nF RF capacitor. Differential resistance, 𝑑𝑉/𝑑𝐼 , data were taken by applying a DC current 𝐼 in addition to a small AC current 𝑑𝐼 = 10 nA at a frequency of 7.189 Hz, using a standard lock-in technique.
